classification_signals: The paper describes a controlled experiment with human subjects (80 undergraduates, p. 6).
It details a 'factorial design' with independent variables (color, visual complexity, orientation) and dependent variables (figure placement, room ratings, p. 6).
It includes a 'METHOD' section with 'SUBJECTS', 'DESIGN', 'PROCEDURE', 'THE MODEL ROOM', and 'DEPENDENT VARIABLES' subsections (pp. 6-9).
It presents 'RESULTS' with statistical analyses (e.g., F-tests, p-values, X2, pp. 10-12).
A 'DISCUSSION' section interprets the findings in relation to predictions and existing theory (pp. 13-16).

limitations: Generalizability is limited by the use of model-room studies, where subjects do not have real experience in the setting.

Visual properties of the setting may assume artificial importance compared to other forms of stimulation (olfactory, tactile) which are absent in model rooms, potentially exaggerating the importance of visual cues.
The elimination of multisensory cues and directly experienced interaction demands in model rooms may hinder a realistic examination of environmental mediation of crowding.
Findings must be replicated in real-life settings before definitive conclusions can be made.
The sample used in this study was relatively homogeneous (e.g., over 80% raised in Metropolitan New York), limiting the possibility of observing differences along certain background characteristics.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated how room color, visual complexity, and social orientation influence perceptions of crowding and room capacity using scaled-down model rooms. Key findings revealed that light-colored rooms were perceived as larger and less crowded, accommodating more figures than dark-colored rooms. While visual complexity and social orientation did not show main effects, significant interactions indicated that high visual complexity increased perceived capacity in social settings (by providing alternative attention loci), but decreased it in dark, nonsocial settings (due to potential sensory overload). The study's generalizability is limited by the use of model rooms, which may overemphasize visual cues and lack real-world multisensory and social interaction, and by a homogeneous subject sample.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The perception and experience of crowding are influenced by environmental cues and social factors, which can intensify or mitigate the effects of physical density.

mechanism_chain.description: Room color influences perceived spaciousness, which in turn affects the perceived capacity of a room and thus the threshold at which crowding is experienced.

instruments_used.description: Behavioral measure of the number of figures placed before a room is considered crowded.
Self-report scale measuring subjective feelings of crowding.
